hints: Compare the group attached to the acidic $O-H$ in each case, a $CH_2Cl$, $CH_2Br$, $CH_3$ with $C=O$ nearby, versus a $CH_2CH_3$ with no $C=O$.
Recall that acidity depends on how easily $H^+$ is lost and how stable the negative ion left behind is.
Think about how electron withdrawing atoms pull electron density away from the $O-H$ bond, and how electron donating alkyl groups push density toward it.
Order Cl versus Br by electronegativity, and remember why any $COOH$ is far more acidic than an $OH$ in an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Sort acids from carboxylic acids to alcohol**
Picture what loses $H^+$. Three compounds have $COOH$ and one has $CH_2OH$. A carboxylate ion, $RCOO^-$, spreads its negative charge over two oxygens by delocalisation, while an alkoxide, $RO^-$, keeps the full charge on one oxygen. That makes any carboxylic acid hugely more acidic than ethanol, so $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is clearly least acidic.

See how halogen substituents help lose $H^+$**
Now compare $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$, $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. When $O-H$ breaks to give $H^+$ plus $RCOO^-$, anything that pulls electrons away helps spread and stabilise that negative charge. Halogens are electronegative, so they exert a negative inductive effect, pulling electron density through sigma bonds, weakening $O-H$ and stabilising the anion.

Put Cl ahead of Br and $CH_3COOH$ last of the acids**
Chlorine is more electronegative than bromine, so $Cl$ withdraws more strongly than $Br$. That makes $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COO}^-$ the most stable anion and $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ the strongest acid, followed by $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$. Ethanoic acid has only a $CH_3$ group which cannot withdraw like a halogen, so it is weakest of the three acids but still stronger than ethanol because it still has the electron withdrawing $C=O$.

Explain why ethanol is so weak**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ there is no $C=O$ to withdraw electrons, and the ethyl group actually pushes electrons toward the $O$ by a positive inductive effect. That strengthens the $O-H$ bond and makes $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ less stable, so ethanol hardly releases $H^+$.

Final answer: most acidic $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ > $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$ > $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ > $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ least acidic.
Electron withdrawing groups exert a negative inductive effect, weakening the $O-H$ bond and stabilising the anion, increasing acidity. Electron donating groups exert a positive inductive effect, strengthening the $O-H$ bond and destabilising the anion, decreasing acidity.
Cl is more electronegative and more electron withdrawing than Br; $C=O$ in $COOH$ is electron withdrawing; alkyl / ethyl group in alcohol is electron donating.

hints: Recall what hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ does to an alkyl side chain on a benzene ring, however long it is.
Recall that ethanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC-COOH}$, is already highly oxidised and is oxidised further to a gas that turns limewater milky.
walkthrough:
Oxidise methylbenzene to benzoic acid**
Hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ is a very strong oxidiser. It oxidises the whole alkyl side chain on the ring right up to the benzylic carbon, leaving $C_6H_5-COOH$. So $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$. The ring itself survives because of its stability.

Oxidise ethanedioic acid to carbon dioxide**
$\text{HOOC-COOH}$ with hot acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ is oxidised completely. Each carbon is already at +3 and goes to +4 in $\text{CO}_2$:
$$\text{(COOH)}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2e^-$$
So the only carbon containing product is $\text{CO}_2$ gas.

Final answer: From methylbenzene: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, benzoic acid (benzene ring with $-COOH$).
From ethanedioic acid: $\text{CO}_2$.

hints: Identify the two reacting groups, $-COOH$ from ethanedioic acid and $-NH_2$ from benzene-1,4-diamine, and recall the link they form with loss of water.
Build one repeat unit containing one phenylene, two $NH$ units and one $-CO-CO-$ unit, with continuation bonds at each end and $C=O$ shown displayed.
walkthrough:
Form the amide link**
A carboxylic acid plus an amine condenses to an amide plus water:
$$\text{-COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{N-} \rightarrow \text{-CO-NH-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Here ethanedioic acid provides $\text{-CO-CO-}$ and benzene-1,4-diamine provides $\text{-NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH-}$.

Draw the repeat unit correctly**
Join them as $\text{---NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH-CO-CO---}$ where the new $\text{-NH-CO-}$ amide groups are shown displayed as $\text{N-H}$ bonded to $\text{C=O}$. Show the phenylene 1,4 substituted, show both $C=O$ double bonds explicitly, and put continuation bonds through the terminal $N$ and terminal $C$ so the chain can extend both ways.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-[NH-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH-CO-CO]-}$ with both $C=O$ displayed, $N$ bonded to phenylene and to $C=O$, and continuation bonds through both ends.

hints: Count that two $-NO_2$ groups each need 6[H] to become $-NH_2$, and balance O atoms as $H_2O$.
walkthrough:
Balance nitro to amine reduction**
Each $\text{-NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{-NH}_2$ needs 6[H] and gives $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. With two nitro groups in 1,4-dinitrobenzene you double everything:
$$\text{O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NO}_2 + 12\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Check atoms: 12 H on left, 4 + 8 = 12 H on right, 4 O on each side.

hints: In step 1 both $-NH_2$ groups in benzene-1,4-diamine are diazotised, so think what $-N_2^+$ group with $Cl^-$ counter ion replaces each one.
In step 2 each diazonium group couples to one phenol molecule in alkaline solution, forming $N=N$ links, so count the carbons in $W$, $C_{18}H_{14}N_4O_2$, to confirm two phenols have added.
walkthrough:
Draw the bis-diazonium salt V**
Step 1 is diazotisation of a diamine, so it happens twice. Each $\text{-NH}_2$ becomes $\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^+$ with a $\text{Cl}^-$ alongside. Keep the central 1,4-phenylene:
$$\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cl}^- \text{ } ^+\text{N}\equiv\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^+ \text{ } \text{Cl}^-$$
That matches formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{N}_4\text{Cl}_2$.

Draw the bis-azo dye W**
In NaOH(aq), phenol couples para to its $OH$ with each diazonium group to give $N=N$. With two ends you get phenol-azo-phenylene-azo-phenol:
$$\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$$
That gives $6+6+6 = 18$ carbons, $4 N$ and $2 O$, matching $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{14}\text{N}_4\text{O}_2$.

Final answer: V: $\text{Cl}^- \text{ } ^+\text{N}\equiv\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^+ \text{ } \text{Cl}^-$, 1,4-benzenebis(diazonium chloride).
W: $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$, central 1,4-phenylene linked by two $N=N$ to two 4-hydroxyphenyl groups (para coupling).

hints: Recall the nitrous acid source made in situ for diazotisation and the critical cold temperature to stop the diazonium ion decomposing.
walkthrough:
Give diazotisation conditions**
Diazotisation needs nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, made in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid. The diazonium ion is unstable and gives off $N_2$ if warmed, so keep the mixture ice cold, below $10\,^\circ\text{C}$:
$$\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl} \text{, } \leqslant 10\,^\circ\text{C}$$
